body:
* **PTHR ID & PTN node:**

GO:0007052 jnm1 mitotic spindle organization
IBA with PTN000394123 , Q13561


* **Sequences with problematic annotation (ID + gene/protein name):**

https://www.pombase.org/gene/SPCC11E10.03


* **Type of Issue: Erroneous source or erroneous propagation, or other issue**

Propagation.
In fission yeast dynactin complex subunits are not expressed during mitosis. They are only expressed during conjugation, and  meiotic prophase. 

* Add the label 'high priority' if needed. Generally high priority issues affect a lot of proteins, and annotations are incorrect (as opposed to just imprecise).

Confirming with Claude:

The Company of Biologists
...three identified dynactin subunits are Arp1, Mug5 (a weak homolog of vertebrate p24), and Jnm1 (also known as Mug1, homologous to p50/dynamitin). The expression of all three — arp1, mug5, and jnm1 — was highly induced in diploid cells starved for nitrogen, indicating that these genes were expressed exclusively in meiotic cells. The same was true for ssm4, encoding the p150Glued subunit. The very names "Mug5" and "Mug1" give it away — "mug" stands for "meiotically upregulated gene," identified through a systematic screen of the meiotic transcriptome of S. pombe. 

Functionally, this fits perfectly. All three dynactin deletion mutants (arp1Δ, jnm1Δ, and mug5Δ) showed no obvious phenotypic alterations during vegetative growth and were not sensitive to the microtubule-depolymerizing drug thiabendazole, suggesting that all three gene products were dispensable for mitotic growth. 

The Company of Biologists
Their defects only showed up in meiosis, where they produced aberrant asci similar to dynein mutants.
The cortical anchor Num1 (Mcp5) follows the same pattern — Num1p is expressed in a meiosis-specific manner and localized to the cell cortex through its C-terminal PH domain. 
PubMed Central

So the whole dynein–dynactin–cortical anchor system in S. pombe appears to be a meiosis-dedicated machinery, primarily powering the horsetail nuclear oscillations needed for homologous chromosome pairing. The fact that these subunits aren't even expressed during vegetative growth makes it very unlikely that dynactin plays any direct role in mitotic spindle assembly in fission yeast — which is a notable difference from the situation in vertebrate cells and even budding yeast, where dynactin components are expressed constitutively and contribute to mitotic spindle positioning.
